Hello,
**My name is Eileen Laubacher, and I am the Democrat and retired U.S. Navy Rear Admiral running against Lauren Boebert here in Colorado.**
I was 17-years-old the first time I raised my right hand and took an oath to support and defend the Constitution against all enemies, foreign and domestic.
I took those words, and that responsibility, seriously every day for the next 4 decades. When I was an intelligence officer. When I was deployed to Afghanistan. When I became an Admiral. And as a member of the president’s National Security Council.
But in all those years, I have never felt as much of a threat to our country, our Constitution, and our very democracy as I do right now. I said I would never run for office. But in this moment, I feel an obligation to step up, serve my community, and defend our country once again.
**I am running for Congress to defeat Lauren Boebert because when she was sworn into office, Lauren took a similar oath to defend our Constitution – and she has betrayed it almost every single day since then.**
Adam Frisch only lost to Lauren Boebert by 546 votes. It was the closest race in the entire country. We can finally put an end to Lauren Boebert’s embarrassing political career – but I need your help now to do it.
Our campaign needs to raise another $50,000 before our deadline at midnight to defeat Lauren Boebert and take back the House for Democrats, but right now, we’re still short. **If I am going to send Lauren Boebert packing and flip this seat blue, I need grassroots donors like you to chip in right now to my campaign:**

Every paycheck in New Mexico gets a bite taken out of it for state income tax. This week, one of the most powerful people in Santa Fe [said out loud what almost no one will](https://us.list-manage.com/R3W0Qwpflc_?e=567664f14c&c2id=f551a60afe6194f7ea2dcf92821ad62e): the state doesn't need a dime of it. Sen. George Muñoz runs the Senate Finance Committee. That's what makes his op-ed impossible to wave off. He opens with the food-bank numbers, then points to one investment figure that quietly makes the whole case for wiping the tax out. Mark says every Republican would vote for it tomorrow.

The real question is what happens when Muñoz's own side reads it.

For months, the biggest names in the party defended Graham Platner through one revelation after another. Then the polls moved — and the same people suddenly rushed for the exits. Scott Jennings says the quiet part out loud about what actually changed. You need to hear it.

**💰 HAALAND'S 7-TO-1 CASH LEAD — AND WHY MARK ISN'T PANICKING
**
The new fundraising numbers are brutal on paper: Deb Haaland is sitting on roughly seven times the cash Gregg Hull has in the bank. But Mark pulls up the 2022 race and finds the one comparison nobody else is making — plus why the Facebook comments tell a very different story. There's a warning in here for Hull. And a reason for hope most people are missing.

WATCHING**

Say what you want about him. In 2016 he made one gamble that reshaped the Supreme Court for a generation — and Mark walks through why even his critics can't dismiss it. Now he's spent weeks in the hospital, and a Kentucky rule most people don't know about decides who fills his seat next.

body:
Peter,
I know it’s late, but I can't stop thinking about how AIPAC, corporate PACs, and a couple of MAGA billionaires could run away with this election simply because they’re outspending us.
It’s something we always knew was coming — and yes, we’re leading in most of the primary and general polls — but it’s still making me nervous.
**I don't want all of our hard work to get erased because a handful of people with more money than sense decided to put their thumb on the scale.** And I wish I didn’t have to constantly be asking for support, but this is the reality of competing in a broken system.
I'm not writing this because I think you haven't done enough, or because I have some perfect ask prepared. I'm writing because it's late, I'm worried, and I trust you enough to just tell you that.
If you're able to pitch in a few bucks tonight, it would mean more to me than I can really put into words right now:

name: Tom Fitton
subject: Judicial Watch Wins January 6 Videos
body:
Charlie Kirk Crime Scene Update

[INSIDE JW]

DC POLICE PRODUCE 1,627 JANUARY 6 BODYCAM VIDEOS

[https://myjw.pr.judicialwatch.org/link.php?AGENCY=jw&M=27089954&N=84041&L=38194&F=T&drurl=aHR0cHM6Ly95b3V0dS5iZS9kOXFHckg3NnliOD91dG1fc291cmNlPWRlcGxveWVyJnV0bV9tZWRpdW09ZW1haWwmdXRtX2NhbXBhaWduPXdlZWtseSt1cGRhdGUmdXRtX3Rlcm09bWVtYmVycyZ1dG1fY29udGVudD1DTWpjd09EazVOVFElM0Q=&hash=db2c21bf0a2f024bb8f53693f9859ac9487329ecaed5902902bb8ea5d321a8f1]

Another victory in our search for the truth of January 6.

The Washington, DC, Metropolitan Police Department released over 1,000
hours of body-worn camera footage in 1,627 videos from the January 6,
2021, U.S. Capitol event. The videos were released because of an April
2026 court ruling
[https://myjw.pr.judicialwatch.org/link.php?AGENCY=jw&M=27089954&N=84041&L=37733&F=T&drurl=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuanVkaWNpYWx3YXRjaC5vcmcvamFudWFyeS02LWJvZHljYW0tZm9vdGFnZS8/dXRtX3NvdXJjZT1kZXBsb3llciZ1dG1fbWVkaXVtPWVtYWlsJnV0bV9jYW1wYWlnbj13ZWVrbHkrdXBkYXRlJnV0bV90ZXJtPW1lbWJlcnMmdXRtX2NvbnRlbnQ9Q01qY3dPRGs1TlRRJTNE&hash=4ae0577c548f0d11fbc7861744548ba92141e4d21608c4dd905d5e056d52c904] in a DC
Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) lawsuit.

The videos are available via our website here
[https://myjw.pr.judicialwatch.org/link.php?AGENCY=jw&M=27089954&N=84041&L=38169&F=T&drurl=aHR0cDovL3d3dy5qdWRpY2lhbHdhdGNoLm9yZy9qYW51YXJ5NmJvZHljYW0/dXRtX3NvdXJjZT1kZXBsb3llciZ1dG1fbWVkaXVtPWVtYWlsJnV0bV9jYW1wYWlnbj13ZWVrbHkrdXBkYXRlJnV0bV90ZXJtPW1lbWJlcnMmdXRtX2NvbnRlbnQ9Q01qY3dPRGs1TlRRJTNE&hash=52f5547be9eb5cf72c76b896f1ae8a07a2dd93bcbb2e06a012c73afe9edcb747]
[https://myjw.pr.judicialwatch.org/link.php?AGENCY=jw&M=27089954&N=84041&L=38168&F=T&drurl=aHR0cDovL3d3dy5qdWRpY2lhbHdhdGNoLm9yZy9qYW51YXJ5NmJvZHljYW1dYW5kP3V0bV9zb3VyY2U9ZGVwbG95ZXImdXRtX21lZGl1bT1lbWFpbCZ1dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249d2Vla2x5K3VwZGF0ZSZ1dG1fdGVybT1tZW1iZXJzJnV0bV9jb250ZW50PUNNamN3T0RrNU5UUSUzRA==&hash=8d7bf55d2f957300efe03d4d17b24475dbb2847081986a2d260218e6b57d029d
https://myjw.pr.judicialwatch.org/link.php?AGENCY=jw&M=27089954&N=84041&L=38169&F=T&drurl=aHR0cDovL3d3dy5qdWRpY2lhbHdhdGNoLm9yZy9qYW51YXJ5NmJvZHljYW0/dXRtX3NvdXJjZT1kZXBsb3llciZ1dG1fbWVkaXVtPWVtYWlsJnV0bV9jYW1wYWlnbj13ZWVrbHkrdXBkYXRlJnV0bV90ZXJtPW1lbWJlcnMmdXRtX2NvbnRlbnQ9Q01qY3dPRGs1TlRRJTNE&hash=52f5547be9eb5cf72c76b896f1ae8a07a2dd93bcbb2e06a012c73afe9edcb747

We filed the DC FOIA lawsuit
[https://myjw.pr.judicialwatch.org/link.php?AGENCY=jw&M=27089954&N=84041&L=32956&F=T&drurl=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuanVkaWNpYWx3YXRjaC5vcmcvZGMtcG9saWNlLWJvZHljYW0tdmlkZW9zLz91dG1fc291cmNlPWRlcGxveWVyJnV0bV9tZWRpdW09ZW1haWwmdXRtX2NhbXBhaWduPXdlZWtseSt1cGRhdGUmdXRtX3Rlcm09bWVtYmVycyZ1dG1fY29udGVudD1DTWpjd09EazVOVFElM0Q=&hash=907f20817f28eb118f5ca5fa3977fbc3567b31096809f7ec768c1d65bd5ba2a4] in June 2024
after the DC Police denied an August 2021 request for all body-worn
camera footage recorded by police officers responding to the January
6, 2021, events at and around the U.S. Capitol (_Judicial Watch v.
District of Columbia_
[https://myjw.pr.judicialwatch.org/link.php?AGENCY=jw&M=27089954&N=84041&L=32934&F=T&drurl=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuanVkaWNpYWx3YXRjaC5vcmcvZG9jdW1lbnRzL2p3LXYtZGMtYm9keWNhbS1mb290YWdlLWNvbXBsYWludC0wMDM0NTMvP3V0bV9zb3VyY2U9ZGVwbG95ZXImdXRtX21lZGl1bT1lbWFpbCZ1dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249d2Vla2x5K3VwZGF0ZSZ1dG1fdGVybT1tZW1iZXJzJnV0bV9jb250ZW50PUNNamN3T0RrNU5UUSUzRA==&hash=e5e997b2211159ba5070a21ea0089468d0d1f45f05f31c189a7ce21c43a7f4e3]
(No. 2024-CAB-003453)).

Earlier this year, a local DC court dealt a major blow to government
secrecy by ruling that the DC Police could not broadly blur and censor
the footage. Rejecting DC Police’s claim that it could withhold
faces and voices of everyone except law enforcement—and its
assertion that producing the footage would cost more than $1.5
million—the court held that any privacy interests were minimal and
outweighed by the overwhelming public interest in disclosure. The
ruling cleared the way for this release of bodycam footage that
documents one of the most consequential events in recent American
history.

The release of these previously secret DC Police January 6 bodycam
videos is the result of a hard-fought victory for transparency by
Judicial Watch. We encourage citizens, law enforcement, Congress and
media to carefully review these videos so they can see more of the
truth about January 6.”

We have conducted a massive, independent investigation into the events
of January 6.

In April 2026, we filed a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) lawsuit
[https://myjw.pr.judicialwatch.org/link.php?AGENCY=jw&M=27089954&N=84041&L=35132&F=T&drurl=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuanVkaWNpYWx3YXRjaC5vcmcvaXJzLXRhcmdldGluZy1vZi1qYW51YXJ5LTYtcHJvdGVzdGVycy8/dXRtX3NvdXJjZT1kZXBsb3llciZ1dG1fbWVkaXVtPWVtYWlsJnV0bV9jYW1wYWlnbj13ZWVrbHkrdXBkYXRlJnV0bV90ZXJtPW1lbWJlcnMmdXRtX2NvbnRlbnQ9Q01qY3dPRGs1TlRRJTNE&hash=d940bf4022f75b18835034a2e1dae54c9cad16b42408012fb3cc3adab09453bf]
against the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) to obtain records related
to possible improper targeting of January 6, 2021, Capitol protesters,
their supporters, and related nonprofits.

In August 2025, we announced that the U.S. Air Force would finally
provide full military funeral honors
[https://myjw.pr.judicialwatch.org/link.php?AGENCY=jw&M=27089954&N=84041&L=35989&F=T&drurl=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuanVkaWNpYWx3YXRjaC5vcmcvZnVuZXJhbC1ob25vcnMtYXNobGktYmFiYml0dC8/dXRtX3NvdXJjZT1kZXBsb3llciZ1dG1fbWVkaXVtPWVtYWlsJnV0bV9jYW1wYWlnbj13ZWVrbHkrdXBkYXRlJnV0bV90ZXJtPW1lbWJlcnMmdXRtX2NvbnRlbnQ9Q01qY3dPRGs1TlRRJTNE&hash=0408f0f78fbd17b8bfc325a5c3d2aff478c86646a12d171f3cbc00bd1db0b8ea] to Ashli
Babbitt, the Air Force veteran who was shot and killed inside the U.S.
Capitol by then-Capitol Police Lt. Michael Byrd on January 6, 2021.
Babbitt was the only official January 6 homicide victim. The Biden
administration had previously denied Babbitt and her family these
honors in retaliation for being at the U.S. Capitol that day. This
decision came on the heels of a massive, nearly $5 million Trump
administration settlement to her family for wrongful death and other
claims against the U.S. Government.

In July 2025, we sued
[https://myjw.pr.judicialwatch.org/link.php?AGENCY=jw&M=27089954&N=84041&L=36077&F=T&drurl=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuanVkaWNpYWx3YXRjaC5vcmcvbGFzdC1taW51dGUtajYtdGFyZ2V0aW5nLz91dG1fc291cmNlPWRlcGxveWVyJnV0bV9tZWRpdW09ZW1haWwmdXRtX2NhbXBhaWduPXdlZWtseSt1cGRhdGUmdXRtX3Rlcm09bWVtYmVycyZ1dG1fY29udGVudD1DTWpjd09EazVOVFElM0Q=&hash=adde74b44353f70814529d5da5700d768029119c3c50d97288bf9bc06c363a18] the U.S.
Department of Justice for records on accelerated January 6
prosecutions after Donald Trump was elected president in November
2024. The Biden administration, anticipating President-elect Donald
Trump’s promise to issue pardons for January 6, 2021, defendants, is
believed to have accelerated prosecutions in the final months of

Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw
Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. That's a nice son! Slowing how fast you age sounds like it should take a punishing diet or a shelf of supplements. New research out of Japan says otherwise. Scientists found that one small daily habit, paired with another, slowed the body's biological aging about as much as cutting your calorie intake by a quarter. In today's _Flyover Podcast_ , Amy shares exactly what the study found, why it surprised the researchers, and what those two simple habits are. [Tune in here to learn more](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykz7FyrCAUgOGngW4dQAQtKG5jt7dNyRzlsJIgOHiyG98-k7xCHuD_Z763u79Dyqk8_sOOjmL1BV9nRiJsPjUoBPnjXGuhVD5xh1IQWvZKKHMT9ialD5Dy5TUPLiIq7Dk6acfeGm2N5JtbJowCYh9Rjxhwhd4YAXYJkx7MMESe3M9NWCmlkEqLzkyrmdSgV2NQqWlkWmBIVFv3XlOhDWO-6hNbt9adZ7cRHSfr_zE1MzU3XBqU0OWLqfmoAb-ogeTNheOVck6nsUyLxw4p__b0J_TTqe8AAAD__6kWa30).****

Have you ever looked at a food label and assumed it was healthy? You're not alone. Nutrition advice seems to change every year, making it harder to know what's actually helping your health. That's why today's sponsor, [Dr. Steven Gundry](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLFuwyAURb8Gb7HggcEeGCpF7tAmQ5eMFoHn5LUYIkxi5e-r9Bc636tzpHM6TAdHkdLl6Ba0dc5Twm2NWCuWiYpL1cWf1edUKd1xcSmhK3ECDnrHzU6IKTiKz0k1wc6IgLJBK0wvjVZGi-ZqZe-hczO60HPFxSAVnFU3ey7PgH3nG7IvGjdCCC5A8VYPXg_QKa81Agw9UxwD1Vza70ypXnGOz_zA0vq8NNFea72tTL4xGBmM27a1Syg3rK-Zwfj1bo7HPYNRfp664ePwusnxToHJveDKMNDr_SyY3JvOiKbYcNsoRlq1YYpfFkfxT1T_Vedh4TcAAP__6tJ0LQ), put together a quick quiz that challenges some of the biggest assumptions about everyday "healthy" snacks. You would think a lifelong Democrat -- someone raised in this party, committed to its stated ideals of civil rights, working people, equality, justice, freedom, and the plain proposition that every person deserves a voice -- would be welcomed in the "big tent."
That is not what happened to me.
I don't especially want to talk about this. I would rather work on what our families need and what we can build together. But people keep asking me what happened during my last campaign -- why the establishment came after me, why a grassroots Democratic leader of a new generation got treated as a threat by her own party. So here's the answer, as plainly as I can give it.
Context: I ran for Congress in 2024. Same seat. Same district. And what happened then tells us a lot about where we are as a country, what lies and misrepresentations prevent actual change, why we aren't where we need to be, and where the changes need to happen to _structurally_ improve our politics: which I believe is, and should be, **the exercise of power in service of responsibility and love for the people.**

## The party is not the people
Call me crazy, but I believe **the support of the people should be the only criterion for democratic legitimacy**. Not whether insiders approve of you. Not whether the consultants find you convenient, or the major donors find you safe, or whether you'll accept the ideological and financial terms set by the people who already hold power. Just the people.
_That 's literally the whole point._
If government "of the people, by the people, for the people" was good enough for Abraham Lincoln as he fought to bring this country back together after the Civil War, it ought to be good enough for the Democratic Party today.
But here's the uncomfortable truth: **America 's political parties are not public democratic institutions**. Legally, they operate a lot more like private clubs -- and they'll tell you so, in open court, when it suits them.
Remember 2016. Bernie Sanders ran an insurgent primary that caught fire -- and then, in its final stretch, thousands of internal DNC emails spilled into public view. They showed party officials, the very people who had sworn up and down they were neutral referees, privately disparaging the Sanders campaign and working to smooth Hillary Clinton's path to the nomination. The fallout was severe enough to force the DNC's chair to resign on the eve of the party's own convention. A group of Democratic voters and donors then sued the DNC over what those emails revealed -- the case is _Wilding v. DNC Services Corp._ Their claim was simple: the DNC's own charter promises that its officers will "maintain impartiality and evenhandedness" during the presidential nominating process, and the party had broken that promise.
You know what the DNC's lawyers argued?
**That the promise didn 't really count.** In open court, they characterized the charter's guarantee of impartiality as "political rhetoric" -- not a real obligation, not something a court could enforce. They said the party had every right, if it wanted, to let its insiders "go into back rooms like they used to and smoke cigars and pick the candidate that way."
Read that again. **The party that sells itself to America as the guardian of democracy stood up in federal court and argued that it was under no enforceable obligation to actually be democratic.**
Y'all. It makes me nauseous.
To the _country 's _credit, the judge didn't buy the spin. He called it a "trivialization" of the DNC's own values and said the party had "committed itself to a higher principle."
_And then he dismissed the case anyway_ -- on the technicality that the voters couldn't prove they'd personally been defrauded. The practical message to every rank-and-file Democrat was the one the court spelled out: your redress is "through the ballot box... not through the judiciary." In other words: trust us, or leave.
And if you're tempted to file this under "2016 was a long time ago" or "that's just sour grapes from the Bernie people" -- don't take my word for it. Take my opponent's.
In July 2024, as the party was in convulsions over whether to keep Joe Biden on the presidential ticket, Congressman Adam Smith -- the 30-year incumbent I am running to unseat -- went on national television and said the quiet part out loud: "**Joe Biden was not picked in 2020 because he was the only person that could beat Donald Trump. He was picked because he was the only person that could beat Bernie Sanders, rightly or wrongly**."[2]
Sit with that, because a sitting congressman just described his own party choosing its presidential nominee not by asking who could best serve the country, and not (heaven forbid!) by listening to the people! - but by asking _who could best stop its own voters ' first choice_.
That wasn't a leak. It wasn't a hack. It wasn't me. That was the man who has held this seat for nearly thirty years, explaining on camera how the machine actually works -- and treating it as the most normal thing in the world. He wasn't "confessing" - he didn't think he was saying anything out of the ordinary. He was describing the water he swims in.
(A necessary aside: I am not letting the Republican Party off the hook. Its escalating racism, its misogyny, its drift toward outright authoritarianism have been more than enough to keep me far away from it. I simply know the Democratic machinery more intimately -- it's the party I was raised in, the party my husband spent decades organizing inside, the one whose inner workings I've now experienced up close. This is _**not**_ a story about Republicans being better. It's a story about one of America's only two political parties failing to be what it tells you it is.)

## Why would they come after me?
Because I represent We the People, and I'm committed to being someone the machinery doesn't control. Because I won't take poison money from corporate, defense, and foreign interests that are against the interests of American communities, profit from our extraction, or benefit from destroying our sovereignty. Because I listen - with real empathy - to voices the insiders would rather manage, deride, or ignore. Because I don't believe disagreement is a threat to democracy -- I believe disagreement _is_ democracy. Listening to people we don't agree with doesn't weaken a society. It's close to the only thing that has ever made one wiser.
But a great deal of party structure isn't built for open deliberation. It's built to **control the outcome** while preserving the _appearance_ of participation. Votes happen. Meetings are held. Committees conduct interviews. Members are allowed to speak.
And yet the decisive questions are usually settled before any of that begins: Who gets to vote? Who appoints the deciders? Who controls the agenda and interprets the rules? Who gets the voter data, the donor lists, the consultants, the infrastructure that decide whether you're even considered "viable"?
I've watched dedicated, principled party members subjected to something close to a public execution -- humiliated, stripped of their positions, driven out -- for the crime of being independent-minded. I've watched coordinated smear campaigns run against people who wouldn't fall in line. Myself included.

## About that time they tried to kill my campaign
When I ran in 2024, as a first-time, grassroots candidate answerable only to the people, **I earned the endorsement of the Veterans and Military Families Caucus of the Washington State Democrats.** (_Side note: in earlier years, the State Dem party had tried to end the system of independent caucuses, because they were**too** independent, too vocal, making their own endorsements and representing the interests of their members. My husband lived through that phase of the Party -- he attended WA State Dems Executive Board meetings for eight years. Popular outcry saved the caucus structure. But that victory was **won** , it wasn't assured._)
Winning that endorsement was a big deal for my campaign. Adam Smith, the incumbent I'm running against, is the Ranking Member (top Democrat) on the House Armed Services Committee, and he's held that position for decades. He has an _**enormous**_ amount of political capital riding on his perceived representation of veterans and military families... but he has _never served in the military, and no one in his family has either_. Unlike me -- a Navy daughter, wife of a wheelchair-bound disabled Army veteran... -- and the caucus went for authentic affinity and genuine support of the people. That was a threat to Adam Smith, and the party's incumbent-protection system that he's embedded in.
Naturally, I immediately started publicizing my endorsement. Running a grassroots campaign, early in the season, we didn't have a lot of money, and we put most of it into printed materials prominently featuring this vote of confidence, among many others.
Then some days later, I got an email from the Washington State Democrats. In it was a letter from the most expensive law firm they have, asserting that **I was falsely claiming the endorsement, that the meeting never happened, and threatening me with a lawsuit** under RCW (Revised Code of Washington) 42.17A.335, which provides for penalties up to and including jail time.
I was the pregnant mother of a toddler at the time, a emerging grassroots leader _of their own party_ ... and out of the blue, they tried to kill my campaign and threatened me with jail time. **I did nothing wrong.**
But here's the real kicker. **They knew it was a lie**. Here's how I know.
Shasti Conrad is the Chair of the Washington State Democrats. She's the top Democratic Party official in the State of Washington. (Since 2024, she has also become Vice Chair of the Democratic National Committee - so now she's #2 in the entire nation.)
Shasti - **herself** \- appointed an acting Chair for that particular meeting, at the 2024 WA State Dems Convention that June weekend in Seattle.
That Acting Chair? A federal attorney named Nick Brown, who won his 2024 campaign and is now **The Attorney General of the State of Washington** , right up there at the top of those leading the legal challenges to the Trump Administration. He took the lead on the legal challenge to Trump's executive order stripping birthright citizenship, on behalf of Washington and a number of other states. He's about the most credible possible Chair of a caucus meeting you could have.
Shasti appointed him as Acting Chair for that meeting. And then **Shasti 's name is on the attorney's letter against me, which claims in black and white that the meeting never happened.**
Couldn't be any clearer: **She knew.**
More than that: the Minutes from that meeting were sent to the Party Affairs director, as well as the Political Advisor Drew Estep, by the Vice-Chair (Joel Ware) within 48 hours of that meeting taking place: June 23rd, 2024. [Here's proof](https://substack.com/redirect/45323685-eba2-453a-93ad-e52137bfac2d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
But then - as the first step in their escalation, that same Senior Advisor Drew Estep emailed me, asserting that the Caucus "has not met this cycle" and that it was "**not possible that your campaign has been endorsed by this Caucus**." (Boldface emphasis in _his_ letter. Evidence [here](https://substack.com/redirect/8f55bc51-2931-4a30-be58-5abe1ef0c258?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).) That email was sent on July 5th, 2024 - nearly two weeks after the Minutes had been emailed to Drew Estep directly.
We have those Minutes from that meeting, showing the appointment of an acting Chair, showing all the normal conduct of meeting business, and confirming my endorsement. They're [here](https://substack.com/redirect/45aa4843-94b9-4750-9e59-67d068b402fe?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
I have the letter from the law firm, with Shasti's name on the cc line, asserting that "the meeting never happened," that I was falsely claiming the endorsement, and threatening me with a lawsuit and jail time _unless I destroyed all my campaign materials that featured the endorsement and sent them proof within 24 hours_ , which amounted to tens of thousands of dollars - most of what we had. Read this letter yourself [here](https://substack.com/redirect/c6c42bcd-e2d7-49c9-ae5b-e026e24f2e0b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
In this particular case, we circulated our evidence, and they backed down. I never got to face them in court.
But let me ask you: _**Wouldn 't you feel deeply hurt, disappointed, and betrayed?**_
I don't share these facts lightly. I'm sharing it because you deserve to understand what an entrenched special interest and advisor within that institution addicted to its own power does when it meets a principled, strong, genuine candidate it can't buy, discipline, absorb, or comfortably control.
I'm not complaining because it happened to me. I'm _**documenting**_ , because if you're sincere, dedicated, and committed to justice, and you try to gain the power required to actually see justice done through one of the only pathways available - _**it will happen to you.**_
Epstein was allowed to operate with impunity as long as he did, because the political bureaucracy was cowed, complicit, bought out, or actively supportive. If we don't _deal with this_ , we're in for more of the same.

## How internal democracy gets engineered away
I've sat through a lot of Democratic endorsement interviews, at the legislative-district and county level. I've won plenty -- and losing an endorsement is nobody's grievance; no candidate is _owed_ one. The problem isn't the outcomes. It's the architecture underneath them.
In a growing number of local party organizations (which are organized at the County level and the LD - Legislative Direct - level, below the State), **the Chair personally appoints five or more members of the Executive Board.** When a Board only seats eight or ten or twelve people, that means whichever faction wins the Chair can hand _itself_ a governing majority by appointment -- not by a vote of the general body.
Ordinary members can want a different direction by a mile and still be structurally locked out of ever electing a majority of the body that speaks in their name.
The same trick runs through endorsements. The Chair or the Board appoints the committee that interviews candidates and decides who gets recommended. And if that committee declines to recommend a candidate, the membership often needs a supermajority -- 60%, sometimes two-thirds, I've even heard 70% -- just to overrule their own committee and endorse you directly.
Sit with that a moment. A handful of people, chosen through a process the leadership already controls, can decline to recommend a grassroots candidate -- and then that candidate has to clear a supermajority of the entire room simply to undo one gatekeeping decision. Let me tell you how hard it is to win two-thirds of a political organization as a newcomer who won't play the transactional game power demands - especially when, in a Congressional race, I have **eleven** LDs to seek endorsement from.
**Now I 've done it, more than once.** But the field is nowhere _close_ to level.
In 2024, the 48th LD overcame a committee recommendation against, and endorsed me - a grassroots challenger of an entrenched incumbent - by a 2:1 ratio.
The 33rd LD, Adam Smith's home district, where he grew up and went to high school - _they_ disavowed him and endorsed me. In fact, they were the very first to do so.
The 31st LD, down in rural Auburn, _rescinded their endorsement_ of Adam Smith and endorsed me.
The 43rd LD Democrats, dense central Seattle, arguably the most powerful in the State of Washington, **formally censured Adam Smith** and endorsed me. (Smith had been making the rounds on TV calling the grassroots protestors for peace and justice and an end to genocide, "left wing authoritarians" and calling for their, and our, arrest and jail time. That type of anti-First Amendment rhetoric has NO place in our politics, **especially** from someone who claims to represent the People, and identifies with the "Democratic" Party.)
This year, the structures have been tightened: among the few LDs that don't have a committee hurdle to clear (where endorsements are voted on directly by the members) many now require a 60% threshold for endorsement, not a simple majority. **In two LDs this year, I have missed the endorsement threshold by 1 vote**. In one case, I won 59.57% of the vote... and despite winning a clear majority and being less than half a percent below their stated endorsement threshold, I did not formally receive that body's endorsement.
It would be maddening, but it's not surprising anymore.
Over the past two years, I've watched these structures tighten, not loosen -- particularly after the surge of grassroots energy in 2024 over genocide and the slaughter of innocent children on our taxpayer dime, and the conduct of Democratic officials.
That is not healthy internal disagreement. That's consolidation.

## "Viability" is manufactured
Then there's everything that happens outside the endorsement room -- because the Party doesn't just hand out a symbolic blessing. **It controls access to the machinery you need to run at all.**
The detailed voter file alone can run tens of thousands of dollars. A professional treasurer familiar with federal compliance regulations -- expensive also. Consultants, tens of thousands each -- and they don't just sell you a service, they function as **gatekeepers** , the toll booths between you and the donors, the power players, the endorsers, the operatives, the friendly press.
They also become security and intelligence vulnerabilities inside your own campaign, and, in my honest opinion, a great deal of the money spent on them is simply wasted. Add polling, digital, advertising, mail, printing, canvassing, text banking, field, compliance -- and a serious Congressional race becomes a seven-figure enterprise fast.
For someone just starting out, accessing voter data for free from the Party is a major gate. If you can clear that hurdle, you have a chance. If you don't, you may not. It's as simple as that.
Party support also provides access to software to run your campaign, free of charge (rather than thousands per month). It also gives you a small army of volunteers... PCOs and other local party members who cheerfully spend their summers canvassing for _whoever their LD endorsed_.
Here in Washington State, I was told that access to the Party's voter file and NGPVan, the main outreach software, was contingent on winning endorsement from over 50% of the LDs within my Congressional district. (Eleven, in my case.)
I had to win 6. I won 4. Against every structural impediment thrown in my way... coming into politics out of nowhere, **I won four.**
**If nothing else, that 's proof that even inside the Party structure, people **_**were**_**and** _**are**_**hungry for real representation**.
But without clearing that threshold, I was locked out of Party infrastructure. So I ran a pedal-to-the-metal grassroots campaign primarily focused on _physical_ outreach: flyers, banners, yard signs, canvassing - inescapable visibility that couldn't be throttled by digital data, deplatformed or shadowbanned online due to my principles, or infiltrated by other campaigns. And I won over 90,000 votes.
Here's what I learned:
**Politics in America is an** _**industry**_**.** A giant economic flywheel of polling, printing, advertising, and consulting - much of it sheer manipulation - fueled by hope and fear and pain and carefully managed narrative. And it is _very good_ at taking brave, decent people and teaching them that survival means becoming part of the machine they came to improve.
Take money from the approved donors. Hire the approved people. Repeat the approved language. Don't challenge the incumbents the party has decided to protect. Don't ask where the money comes from. Don't get unpredictable.
I'm what that machine chokes on.

## Incumbency has become a guarantee
All of this matters because the United States has built one of the most powerful systems of incumbent protection in the democratic world.
In recent Congressional elections, House incumbents who run for reelection win around 95% of the time. Or more. That's not just a healthy advantage of experience and name recognition. That's a near-guarantee.
Safe seats, gerrymandered maps to keep the incumbent (or at least the same party) in power over decades, single-member districts decided in low-turnout primaries, decades-deep donor relationships, and a press that treats incumbents as the default and challengers as curiosities -- the advantages stack on advantages until the election is competitive in form and settled in fact. Without the party's backing, or a coordinated retirement in which leadership decides it's finally time to open a seat (to whomever they approve...), a challenger faces _very long odds._
Which means the Party gets to decide who's "viable." It can quietly require you to accept a particular line, a particular funding model, a particular set of loyalties -- not to mention, particular entrenched advisors who've come from the Party itself. (The revolving door is real, at all levels.)
Toe the line, and the blessings of praise, support, and access to power are showered upon you. Refuse, and you're thrown to the wolves.
That's what happened to me.
Healthier democracies aren't like this. Incumbency still helps in them -- experience should count for something -- but across comparable Western parliaments, incumbent reelection rates tend to run closer to 70%. Not like ours, at 95%+.
The distance between "a real advantage" and "a near-lock" is the distance between a genuine competitive democracy and what political scientists have called _congressional stagnation_ : a system that holds individual officeholders in place at rates that look less like representation and more like fiefdoms -- even as the public's approval of Congress sits in the basement.

## This is how a government grows old and stops working
You can see the cost in the age and condition of Congress itself.
The average member of the House is now approaching 60. The average senator is in his or her mid-60s -- right around the age the rest of the country calls retirement.
And those are _averages_. Roughly two dozen members of Congress are 80 or older. More than half the Senate is over 60. A handful of Senators are in their 80s, including one who's been MIA for weeks now, and one - **an active, sitting Senator, Chuck Grassley, is in his 90s.**
In most functioning legislatures around the world, lawmakers run about 8-10 years older than the average of the people they serve. In ours, that gap is closer to 18-20 years.
There is nothing wrong with an older person serving. Age brings memory, judgment, and hard-won wisdom, and I want all of that in our government. The problem isn't that elders serve. The problem is a system with _so little turnover_ that people are pressured to _stay_ -- long past the point a healthy institution would have raised up successors -- because there's no dignified path out, and no one waiting to take the baton who was ever allowed to.
Colloquially speaking, our politics eats its own young.
And so the baton gets passed the hardest way there is. Since 2016, 21 Senators and Representatives have died in office. 14 of them were Democrats. That is not an indictment of any one of those individuals necessarily; many were extraordinary public servants, and I mourn them. It is an indictment of a political culture that has forgotten how to let go.
Look at what's happening even as I write this. One of the most powerful men in the Senate has been hospitalized for weeks under circumstances his own office won't explain -- to the point that his home-state Governor has had to publicly demand basic information about whether the people of that state are being represented at all. Whatever you think of his politics, and you know what I think of them, no Constitutional Republic should run this way.
A seat in Congress is not a possession to be held tightly until your last breath. **It is a public trust, lent by the people, meant to be handed on in turn.**
That is what a healthy government and party system would understand. Instead, too often, ours behaves like a ratchet. Republicans drag the country right; [corporate-aligned Democrats](https://substack.com/redirect/e841b500-094b-44a2-8639-1870fb1491e7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) keep it from moving meaningfully back; and the machinery locks the result in place and calls it pragmatism.
That's how a country destroys its own future. That's how political imagination dies. That's how people stop believing the whole system can ever answer them again.

## What we can actually change
The single most direct fix is congressional term limits. I support a hard cap -- 12 years in the House, 18 in the Senate. Long enough to build real expertise, real relationships, and a real record. _Not long enough to turn a public office into private property._ Term limits guarantee the openings that let new leaders rise, they keep advantage from compounding forever, and they force the parties to _develop_ successors instead of protecting incumbents until scandal or death does the job for them.
Term limits alone won't do it, though. We also need **independent redistricting** , so voters pick their representatives instead of representatives picking their voters. **Ranked-choice voting,** so people can vote their conscience without being trapped by "spoilers." **Public campaign financing** and equal, **affordable access to voter data,** so a good candidate with no rich friends can still reach the people, make their case, and offer their service.
And inside the parties themselves: **legal accountability,** transparent bylaws, governing boards elected directly by the membership, strict limits on appointed seats, lower thresholds for members to overrule their own committees, real protection for caucuses and dissenting voices, and open records for endorsement votes and internal discipline.
The answer, I believe, is not to burn political organization down. Parties, at their best, are how people gather, deliberate, teach one another, recruit candidates, build coalitions, and turn shared values into governing power. That's the reason we built them.
**The answer is to make them belong to the people again.**

## What I still believe
**I believe in democracy**. Not the branding. Not the ceremonies. Not the carefully managed performance of participation -- _the real thing_.
People thinking together. People disagreeing honestly. People coming to agreement where they can, and genuinely competing fairly in public when they cannot. People choosing who represents them, and removing them when they stop serving the public's interest. People handing knowledge and responsibility from one generation to the next, on purpose, with grace.
_**Government of the people, by the people, and for the people.**_
That should not be a radical demand inside the Democratic Party. It should be the minimum requirement for using the name.
Care. Courage. The Constitution

Why the Democratic Party treated a lifelong Democrat as a threat -- threatened me with a lawsuit and jail time over a lie -- and what it taught me about the machine we're up against, & steps to fix it. | | | Jul 11 | | | | | | | | | | | | You would think a lifelong Democrat -- someone raised in this party, committed to its stated ideals of civil rights, working people, equality, justice, freedom, and the plain proposition that every person deserves a voice -- would be welcomed in the "big tent." That is not what happened to me. I don't especially want to talk about this. I would rather work on what our families need and what we can build together. But people keep asking me what happened during my last campaign -- why the establishment came after me, why a grassroots Democratic leader of a new generation got treated as a threat by her own party. So here's the answer, as plainly as I can give it. Context: I ran for Congress in 2024. Same seat. Same district. And what happened then tells us a lot about where we are as a country, what lies and misrepresentations prevent actual change, why we aren't where we need to be, and where the changes need to happen to structurally improve our politics: which I believe is, and should be, the exercise of power in service of responsibility and love for the people. | | ---|---|--- The party is not the people Call me crazy, but I believe the support of the people should be the only criterion for democratic legitimacy. Not whether insiders approve of you. Not whether the consultants find you convenient, or the major donors find you safe, or whether you'll accept the ideological and financial terms set by the people who already hold power. Just the people. That 's literally the whole point. If government "of the people, by the people, for the people" was good enough for Abraham Lincoln as he fought to bring this country back together after the Civil War, it ought to be good enough for the Democratic Party today. But here's the uncomfortable truth: America 's political parties are not public democratic institutions. Legally, they operate a lot more like private clubs -- and they'll tell you so, in open court, when it suits them. Remember 2016. Bernie Sanders ran an insurgent primary that caught fire -- and then, in its final stretch, thousands of internal DNC emails spilled into public view. They showed party officials, the very people who had sworn up and down they were neutral referees, privately disparaging the Sanders campaign and working to smooth Hillary Clinton's path to the nomination. The fallout was severe enough to force the DNC's chair to resign on the eve of the party's own convention. A group of Democratic voters and donors then sued the DNC over what those emails revealed -- the case is Wilding v. DNC Services Corp. Their claim was simple: the DNC's own charter promises that its officers will "maintain impartiality and evenhandedness" during the presidential nominating process, and the party had broken that promise. You know what the DNC's lawyers argued? That the promise didn 't really count. In open court, they characterized the charter's guarantee of impartiality as "political rhetoric" -- not a real obligation, not something a court could enforce. They said the party had every right, if it wanted, to let its insiders "go into back rooms like they used to and smoke cigars and pick the candidate that way." Read that again. The party that sells itself to America as the guardian of democracy stood up in federal court and argued that it was under no enforceable obligation to actually be democratic. Y'all. It makes me nauseous. To the country 's credit, the judge didn't buy the spin. He called it a "trivialization" of the DNC's own values and said the party had "committed itself to a higher principle." And then he dismissed the case anyway -- on the technicality that the voters couldn't prove they'd personally been defrauded. The practical message to every rank-and-file Democrat was the one the court spelled out: your redress is "through the ballot box... not through the judiciary." In other words: trust us, or leave. And if you're tempted to file this under "2016 was a long time ago" or "that's just sour grapes from the Bernie people" -- don't take my word for it. Take my opponent's. In July 2024, as the party was in convulsions over whether to keep Joe Biden on the presidential ticket, Congressman Adam Smith -- the 30-year incumbent I am running to unseat -- went on national television and said the quiet part out loud: "Joe Biden was not picked in 2020 because he was the only person that could beat Donald Trump. He was picked because he was the only person that could beat Bernie Sanders, rightly or wrongly."[2] Sit with that, because a sitting congressman just described his own party choosing its presidential nominee not by asking who could best serve the country, and not (heaven forbid!) by listening to the people! - but by asking who could best stop its own voters ' first choice. That wasn't a leak. It wasn't a hack. It wasn't me. That was the man who has held this seat for nearly thirty years, explaining on camera how the machine actually works -- and treating it as the most normal thing in the world. He wasn't "confessing" - he didn't think he was saying anything out of the ordinary. He was describing the water he swims in. (A necessary aside: I am not letting the Republican Party off the hook. Its escalating racism, its misogyny, its drift toward outright authoritarianism have been more than enough to keep me far away from it. I simply know the Democratic machinery more intimately -- it's the party I was raised in, the party my husband spent decades organizing inside, the one whose inner workings I've now experienced up close. This is not a story about Republicans being better. It's a story about one of America's only two political parties failing to be what it tells you it is.) Why would they come after me? Because I represent We the People, and I'm committed to being someone the machinery doesn't control. Because I won't take poison money from corporate, defense, and foreign interests that are against the interests of American communities, profit from our extraction, or benefit from destroying our sovereignty. Because I listen - with real empathy - to voices the insiders would rather manage, deride, or ignore. Because I don't believe disagreement is a threat to democracy -- I believe disagreement is democracy. Listening to people we don't agree with doesn't weaken a society. It's close to the only thing that has ever made one wiser. But a great deal of party structure isn't built for open deliberation. It's built to control the outcome while preserving the appearance of participation. Votes happen. Meetings are held. Committees conduct interviews. Members are allowed to speak. And yet the decisive questions are usually settled before any of that begins: Who gets to vote? Who appoints the deciders? Who controls the agenda and interprets the rules? Who gets the voter data, the donor lists, the consultants, the infrastructure that decide whether you're even considered "viable"? I've watched dedicated, principled party members subjected to something close to a public execution -- humiliated, stripped of their positions, driven out -- for the crime of being independent-minded. I've watched coordinated smear campaigns run against people who wouldn't fall in line. Myself included. | | ---|---|--- About that time they tried to kill my campaign When I ran in 2024, as a first-time, grassroots candidate answerable only to the people, I earned the endorsement of the Veterans and Military Families Caucus of the Washington State Democrats. (Side note: in earlier years, the State Dem party had tried to end the system of independent caucuses, because they weretoo independent, too vocal, making their own endorsements and representing the interests of their members. My husband lived through that phase of the Party -- he attended WA State Dems Executive Board meetings for eight years. Popular outcry saved the caucus structure. But that victory was won , it wasn't assured.) Winning that endorsement was a big deal for my campaign. Adam Smith, the incumbent I'm running against, is the Ranking Member (top Democrat) on the House Armed Services Committee, and he's held that position for decades. He has an enormous amount of political capital riding on his perceived representation of veterans and military families... but he has never served in the military, and no one in his family has either. Unlike me -- a Navy daughter, wife of a wheelchair-bound disabled Army veteran... -- and the caucus went for authentic affinity and genuine support of the people. That was a threat to Adam Smith, and the party's incumbent-protection system that he's embedded in. Naturally, I immediately started publicizing my endorsement. Running a grassroots campaign, early in the season, we didn't have a lot of money, and we put most of it into printed materials prominently featuring this vote of confidence, among many others. Then some days later, I got an email from the Washington State Democrats. In it was a letter from the most expensive law firm they have, asserting that I was falsely claiming the endorsement, that the meeting never happened, and threatening me with a lawsuit under RCW (Revised Code of Washington) 42.17A.335, which provides for penalties up to and including jail time. I was the pregnant mother of a toddler at the time, a emerging grassroots leader of their own party ... and out of the blue, they tried to kill my campaign and threatened me with jail time. I did nothing wrong. But here's the real kicker. They knew it was a lie. Here's how I know. Shasti Conrad is the Chair of the Washington State Democrats. She's the top Democratic Party official in the State of Washington. (Since 2024, she has also become Vice Chair of the Democratic National Committee - so now she's #2 in the entire nation.) Shasti - herself \- appointed an acting Chair for that particular meeting, at the 2024 WA State Dems Convention that June weekend in Seattle. That Acting Chair? A federal attorney named Nick Brown, who won his 2024 campaign and is now The Attorney General of the State of Washington , right up there at the top of those leading the legal challenges to the Trump Administration. He took the lead on the legal challenge to Trump's executive order stripping birthright citizenship, on behalf of Washington and a number of other states. He's about the most credible possible Chair of a caucus meeting you could have. Shasti appointed him as Acting Chair for that meeting. And then Shasti 's name is on the attorney's letter against me, which claims in black and white that the meeting never happened. Couldn't be any clearer: She knew. More than that: the Minutes from that meeting were sent to the Party Affairs director, as well as the Political Advisor Drew Estep, by the Vice-Chair (Joel Ware) within 48 hours of that meeting taking place: June 23rd, 2024. . But then - as the first step in their escalation, that same Senior Advisor Drew Estep emailed me, asserting that the Caucus "has not met this cycle" and that it was "not possible that your campaign has been endorsed by this Caucus." (Boldface emphasis in his letter. Evidence .) That email was sent on July 5th, 2024 - nearly two weeks after the Minutes had been emailed to Drew Estep directly. We have those Minutes from that meeting, showing the appointment of an acting Chair, showing all the normal conduct of meeting business, and confirming my endorsement. They're . I have the letter from the law firm, with Shasti's name on the cc line, asserting that "the meeting never happened," that I was falsely claiming the endorsement, and threatening me with a lawsuit and jail time unless I destroyed all my campaign materials that featured the endorsement and sent them proof within 24 hours , which amounted to tens of thousands of dollars - most of what we had. Read this letter yourself . In this particular case, we circulated our evidence, and they backed down. I never got to face them in court. But let me ask you: Wouldn 't you feel deeply hurt, disappointed, and betrayed? I don't share these facts lightly. I'm sharing it because you deserve to understand what an entrenched special interest and advisor within that institution addicted to its own power does when it meets a principled, strong, genuine candidate it can't buy, discipline, absorb, or comfortably control. I'm not complaining because it happened to me. I'm documenting , because if you're sincere, dedicated, and committed to justice, and you try to gain the power required to actually see justice done through one of the only pathways available - it will happen to you. Epstein was allowed to operate with impunity as long as he did, because the political bureaucracy was cowed, complicit, bought out, or actively supportive. If we don't deal with this , we're in for more of the same. How internal democracy gets engineered away I've sat through a lot of Democratic endorsement interviews, at the legislative-district and county level. I've won plenty -- and losing an endorsement is nobody's grievance; no candidate is owed one. The problem isn't the outcomes. It's the architecture underneath them. In a growing number of local party organizations (which are organized at the County level and the LD - Legislative Direct - level, below the State), the Chair personally appoints five or more members of the Executive Board. When a Board only seats eight or ten or twelve people, that means whichever faction wins the Chair can hand itself a governing majority by appointment -- not by a vote of the general body. Ordinary members can want a different direction by a mile and still be structurally locked out of ever electing a majority of the body that speaks in their name. The same trick runs through endorsements. The Chair or the Board appoints the committee that interviews candidates and decides who gets recommended. And if that committee declines to recommend a candidate, the membership often needs a supermajority -- 60%, sometimes two-thirds, I've even heard 70% -- just to overrule their own committee and endorse you directly. Sit with that a moment. A handful of people, chosen through a process the leadership already controls, can decline to recommend a grassroots candidate -- and then that candidate has to clear a supermajority of the entire room simply to undo one gatekeeping decision. Let me tell you how hard it is to win two-thirds of a political organization as a newcomer who won't play the transactional game power demands - especially when, in a Congressional race, I have eleven LDs to seek endorsement from. Now I 've done it, more than once. But the field is nowhere close to level. In 2024, the 48th LD overcame a committee recommendation against, and endorsed me - a grassroots challenger of an entrenched incumbent - by a 2:1 ratio. The 33rd LD, Adam Smith's home district, where he grew up and went to high school - they disavowed him and endorsed me. In fact, they were the very first to do so. The 31st LD, down in rural Auburn, rescinded their endorsement of Adam Smith and endorsed me. The 43rd LD Democrats, dense central Seattle, arguably the most powerful in the State of Washington, formally censured Adam Smith and endorsed me. (Smith had been making the rounds on TV calling the grassroots protestors for peace and justice and an end to genocide, "left wing authoritarians" and calling for their, and our, arrest and jail time. That type of anti-First Amendment rhetoric has NO place in our politics, especially from someone who claims to represent the People, and identifies with the "Democratic" Party.) This year, the structures have been tightened: among the few LDs that don't have a committee hurdle to clear (where endorsements are voted on directly by the members) many now require a 60% threshold for endorsement, not a simple majority. In two LDs this year, I have missed the endorsement threshold by 1 vote. In one case, I won 59.57% of the vote... and despite winning a clear majority and being less than half a percent below their stated endorsement threshold, I did not formally receive that body's endorsement. It would be maddening, but it's not surprising anymore. Over the past two years, I've watched these structures tighten, not loosen -- particularly after the surge of grassroots energy in 2024 over genocide and the slaughter of innocent children on our taxpayer dime, and the conduct of Democratic officials. That is not healthy internal disagreement. That's consolidation. | | ---|---|--- "Viability" is manufactured Then there's everything that happens outside the endorsement room -- because the Party doesn't just hand out a symbolic blessing. It controls access to the machinery you need to run at all. The detailed voter file alone can run tens of thousands of dollars. A professional treasurer familiar with federal compliance regulations -- expensive also. Consultants, tens of thousands each -- and they don't just sell you a service, they function as gatekeepers , the toll booths between you and the donors, the power players, the endorsers, the operatives, the friendly press. They also become security and intelligence vulnerabilities inside your own campaign, and, in my honest opinion, a great deal of the money spent on them is simply wasted. Add polling, digital, advertising, mail, printing, canvassing, text banking, field, compliance -- and a serious Congressional race becomes a seven-figure enterprise fast. For someone just starting out, accessing voter data for free from the Party is a major gate. If you can clear that hurdle, you have a chance. If you don't, you may not. It's as simple as that. Party support also provides access to software to run your campaign, free of charge (rather than thousands per month). It also gives you a small army of volunteers... PCOs and other local party members who cheerfully spend their summers canvassing for whoever their LD endorsed. Here in Washington State, I was told that access to the Party's voter file and NGPVan, the main outreach software, was contingent on winning endorsement from over 50% of the LDs within my Congressional district. (Eleven, in my case.) I had to win 6. I won 4. Against every structural impediment thrown in my way... coming into politics out of nowhere, I won four. If nothing else, that 's proof that even inside the Party structure, people wereand arehungry for real representation. But without clearing that threshold, I was locked out of Party infrastructure. So I ran a pedal-to-the-metal grassroots campaign primarily focused on physical outreach: flyers, banners, yard signs, canvassing - inescapable visibility that couldn't be throttled by digital data, deplatformed or shadowbanned online due to my principles, or infiltrated by other campaigns. And I won over 90,000 votes. Here's what I learned: Politics in America is an industry. A giant economic flywheel of polling, printing, advertising, and consulting - much of it sheer manipulation - fueled by hope and fear and pain and carefully managed narrative. And it is very good at taking brave, decent people and teaching them that survival means becoming part of the machine they came to improve. Take money from the approved donors. Hire the approved people. Repeat the approved language. Don't challenge the incumbents the party has decided to protect. Don't ask where the money comes from. Don't get unpredictable. I'm what that machine chokes on. Incumbency has become a guarantee All of this matters because the United States has built one of the most powerful systems of incumbent protection in the democratic world. In recent Congressional elections, House incumbents who run for reelection win around 95% of the time. Or more. That's not just a healthy advantage of experience and name recognition. That's a near-guarantee. Safe seats, gerrymandered maps to keep the incumbent (or at least the same party) in power over decades, single-member districts decided in low-turnout primaries, decades-deep donor relationships, and a press that treats incumbents as the default and challengers as curiosities -- the advantages stack on advantages until the election is competitive in form and settled in fact. Without the party's backing, or a coordinated retirement in which leadership decides it's finally time to open a seat (to whomever they approve...), a challenger faces very long odds. Which means the Party gets to decide who's "viable." It can quietly require you to accept a particular line, a particular funding model, a particular set of loyalties -- not to mention, particular entrenched advisors who've come from the Party itself. (The revolving door is real, at all levels.) Toe the line, and the blessings of praise, support, and access to power are showered upon you. Refuse, and you're thrown to the wolves. That's what happened to me. Healthier democracies aren't like this. Incumbency still helps in them -- experience should count for something -- but across comparable Western parliaments, incumbent reelection rates tend to run closer to 70%. Not like ours, at 95%+. The distance between "a real advantage" and "a near-lock" is the distance between a genuine competitive democracy and what political scientists have called congressional stagnation : a system that holds individual officeholders in place at rates that look less like representation and more like fiefdoms -- even as the public's approval of Congress sits in the basement. | | ---|---|--- This is how a government grows old and stops working You can see the cost in the age and condition of Congress itself. The average member of the House is now approaching 60. The average senator is in his or her mid-60s -- right around the age the rest of the country calls retirement. And those are averages. Roughly two dozen members of Congress are 80 or older. More than half the Senate is over 60. A handful of Senators are in their 80s, including one who's been MIA for weeks now, and one - an active, sitting Senator, Chuck Grassley, is in his 90s. In most functioning legislatures around the world, lawmakers run about 8-10 years older than the average of the people they serve. In ours, that gap is closer to 18-20 years. There is nothing wrong with an older person serving. Age brings memory, judgment, and hard-won wisdom, and I want all of that in our government. The problem isn't that elders serve. The problem is a system with so little turnover that people are pressured to stay -- long past the point a healthy institution would have raised up successors -- because there's no dignified path out, and no one waiting to take the baton who was ever allowed to. Colloquially speaking, our politics eats its own young. And so the baton gets passed the hardest way there is. Since 2016, 21 Senators and Representatives have died in office. 14 of them were Democrats. That is not an indictment of any one of those individuals necessarily; many were extraordinary public servants, and I mourn them. It is an indictment of a political culture that has forgotten how to let go. Look at what's happening even as I write this. One of the most powerful men in the Senate has been hospitalized for weeks under circumstances his own office won't explain -- to the point that his home-state Governor has had to publicly demand basic information about whether the people of that state are being represented at all. Whatever you think of his politics, and you know what I think of them, no Constitutional Republic should run this way. A seat in Congress is not a possession to be held tightly until your last breath. It is a public trust, lent by the people, meant to be handed on in turn. That is what a healthy government and party system would understand. Instead, too often, ours behaves like a ratchet. Republicans drag the country right; keep it from moving meaningfully back; and the machinery locks the result in place and calls it pragmatism. That's how a country destroys its own future. That's how political imagination dies. That's how people stop believing the whole system can ever answer them again. What we can actually change The single most direct fix is congressional term limits. I support a hard cap -- 12 years in the House, 18 in the Senate. Long enough to build real expertise, real relationships, and a real record. Not long enough to turn a public office into private property. Term limits guarantee the openings that let new leaders rise, they keep advantage from compounding forever, and they force the parties to develop successors instead of protecting incumbents until scandal or death does the job for them. Term limits alone won't do it, though. We also need independent redistricting , so voters pick their representatives instead of representatives picking their voters. Ranked-choice voting, so people can vote their conscience without being trapped by "spoilers." Public campaign financing and equal, affordable access to voter data, so a good candidate with no rich friends can still reach the people, make their case, and offer their service. And inside the parties themselves: legal accountability, transparent bylaws, governing boards elected directly by the membership, strict limits on appointed seats, lower thresholds for members to overrule their own committees, real protection for caucuses and dissenting voices, and open records for endorsement votes and internal discipline. The answer, I believe, is not to burn political organization down. Parties, at their best, are how people gather, deliberate, teach one another, recruit candidates, build coalitions, and turn shared values into governing power. That's the reason we built them. The answer is to make them belong to the people again. | | ---|---|--- What I still believe I believe in democracy. Not the branding. Not the ceremonies. Not the carefully managed performance of participation -- the real thing. People thinking together. People disagreeing honestly. People coming to agreement where they can, and genuinely competing fairly in public when they cannot. People choosing who represents them, and removing them when they stop serving the public's interest. People handing knowledge and responsibility from one generation to the next, on purpose, with grace. Government of the people, by the people, and for the people. That should not be a radical demand inside the Democratic Party. It should be the minimum requirement for using the name. Care. Courage.
